lead: A wall footing, or strip footing, is a long reinforced concrete slab under a load-bearing wall. It widens the wall's narrow base so the soil pressure stays below the safe bearing capacity. Each metre of wall is designed as a pair of cantilevers sticking out on both sides of the wall: the width comes from the soil, the depth from one-way shear and bending, and the steel from bending across the width. Only a few syllabi list it as a separate topic, but where it appears it is a standard long design question. You see it under brick compound walls, load-bearing houses and the walls of small sheds.
prereq: You need singly reinforced section design and the shear strength τ<sub>c</sub> of IS 456 Table 19 (see Singly reinforced rectangular beams and Design of shear reinforcement).

sections.h3: Width, pressure and the critical sections

blocks.text: Take 1 m length of wall. With service load P (kN/m, wall plus what it carries) and safe bearing capacity qs (kN/m²), the width is B = (P + footing weight)/qs; the footing weight is often taken as 10 % of P at first and checked later. The soil pushes up on the slab with the net factored pressure wu = 1.5P/B. The footing's own weight is left out of wu: it sits directly on the soil and causes no bending.

blocks.where: lm is the distance from the free edge to the critical section for moment. IS 456 clause 34.2.3.2 puts that section at the face of a concrete wall, but halfway between the centre-line and the face of a masonry wall, so for a brick wall lm = (B − t)/2 + t/4, where t is the wall thickness.

blocks.text: The reason for the masonry rule: a brick wall is not monolithic with the footing, so it does not stiffen the slab right up to its face. One-way shear is checked at distance d (the effective depth) from the face of the wall, with V<sub>u</sub> = w<sub>u</sub>((B − t)/2 − d). Punching shear does not arise for a continuous wall.

items: Depth for bending: d ≥ √(M<sub>u</sub>/(0.138f<sub>ck</sub> × 1000)) for Fe415. Footings are usually made deeper than this so that one-way shear passes without stirrups (IS 456 expects footings to carry shear by concrete alone in ordinary cases).
Main steel across the width from M<sub>u</sub> = 0.87f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>st</sub>d(1 − f<sub>y</sub>A<sub>st</sub>/(f<sub>ck</sub>bd)), not less than 0.12 % of the gross section for Fe415.

Development length: each bar must extend L<sub>d</sub> = 0.87f<sub>y</sub>φ/(4τ<sub>bd</sub>) beyond the critical section for moment. For M20 and Fe415, τ<sub>bd</sub> = 1.2 × 1.6 = 1.92 N/mm², so L<sub>d</sub> = 47φ.
Distribution steel along the wall: 0.12 % of the gross section.
Thickness at the edge at least 150 mm (IS 456 clause 34.1.2); the top may slope from the wall to the edge to save concrete. Clear cover 50 mm, on a 75 to 100 mm bed of lean concrete.

examples.question: A 230 mm brick wall carries a service load of 160 kN per metre. The safe bearing capacity is 150 kN/m². Design the footing in M20 concrete with Fe415 bars.
steps: Width: allow 10 % for self-weight, B = 1.1 × 160/150 = 1.17 m. Adopt B = 1.20 m.
Net factored pressure: w<sub>u</sub> = 1.5 × 160/1.20 = 200 kN/m². Projection from the wall face: (1.20 − 0.23)/2 = 0.485 m.

Critical section for moment (masonry wall): 0.485 + 0.23/4 = 0.5425 m from the free edge. M<sub>u</sub> = 200 × 0.5425²/2 = 29.43 kN·m per metre. (Taken at the face, as for a concrete wall, it would be only 23.52 kN·m.)
Depth for bending: d = √(29.43 × 10⁶/(0.138 × 20 × 1000)) = 103.3 mm. Adopt D = 250 mm with 10 mm bars: d = 250 − 50 − 5 = 195 mm.
Steel: A<sub>st</sub> = 438 mm²/m (minimum 0.0012 × 1000 × 250 = 300 mm²/m). Provide 10 mm at 175 mm c/c: 449 mm²/m, p<sub>t</sub> = 0.230 %.

One-way shear at d from the face: x = 0.485 − 0.195 = 0.290 m, V<sub>u</sub> = 200 × 0.290 = 58.0 kN/m, τ<sub>v</sub> = 58000/(1000 × 195) = 0.297 N/mm². τ<sub>c</sub> for p<sub>t</sub> = 0.23 % (M20) = 0.344 N/mm² > τ<sub>v</sub>. Safe.
Development length of 10 mm bars: 47 × 10 = 470 mm. Available beyond the critical section: 542.5 − 50 = 492.5 mm ≥ 470 mm. (A 12 mm bar would need 564 mm, more than available, unless bent up.)
Distribution: 0.0012 × 1000 × 250 = 300 mm²/m; provide 8 mm at 160 mm c/c (314 mm²/m).
Soil check with the real self-weight: (160 + 0.25 × 1.2 × 25)/1.2 = 139.6 kN/m² ≤ 150. Safe.
examples.answer: B = 1.2 m, D = 250 mm; 10 mm bars at 175 mm c/c across the width and 8 mm at 160 mm c/c along the wall; one-way shear 0.30 < 0.34 N/mm².

traps: Taking the moment at the face of a brick wall. For masonry the section is halfway between the centre-line and the face (t/4 inside the face), which gives the larger moment.
Putting the footing's self-weight into w<sub>u</sub>. It is counted for bearing, not for bending or shear.
Using the service pressure (here 133 kN/m²) with factored moments.
Adding stirrups to a thin footing that fails in shear. Make the footing deeper instead.
Forgetting the development length: a large bar can fail to anchor in a short projection.

quiz.q: Where is the critical section for bending in a footing under (a) a concrete wall, (b) a brick wall?
quiz.a: (a) At the face of the wall. (b) Halfway between the centre-line and the face of the wall.

quiz.q: Why is the footing's own weight left out of the net upward pressure used for design?
quiz.a: The weight of each part of the slab sits directly on the soil under it, so the soil reaction to it cancels at every point and causes no shear or bending. Only the wall load bends the slab.

quiz.q: A wall carries 150 kN/m on soil of safe bearing capacity 100 kN/m². Find B allowing 10 % for self-weight.
For a 300 mm concrete wall on a 1.5 m footing with w<sub>u</sub> = 180 kN/m², find M<sub>u</sub>.
quiz.a: Projection (1.5 − 0.3)/2 = 0.6 m, at the face for a concrete wall. M<sub>u</sub> = 180 × 0.6²/2 = 32.4 kN·m/m.

quiz.q: In the worked example, find the one-way shear stress if D were 200 mm (d = 145 mm).
quiz.a: x = 0.485 − 0.145 = 0.340 m, V<sub>u</sub> = 200 × 0.340 = 68.0 kN/m, τ<sub>v</sub> = 68 000/(1000 × 145) = 0.469 N/mm², above τ<sub>c</sub> = 0.39 N/mm² for the same bars (p<sub>t</sub> = 0.31 %), so 200 mm is too thin.

quiz.q: Why does the masonry-wall rule give a larger moment than the face rule, and when does it matter most?
quiz.a: It moves the section t/4 towards the wall centre, so the lever arm grows from (B − t)/2 to (B − t)/2 + t/4. It matters most for thick walls on narrow footings: in the worked example it raises M<sub>u</sub> from 23.5 to 29.4 kN·m/m, a quarter more.

beyond: Not for the exam. Where a wall stands on a property line, the footing cannot project outside it and becomes eccentric; designers then use a strap beam to an inner footing. On soft clay, long wall footings are often replaced by grade beams on short bored piles. Search for "strap footing", "grade beam on piles" and "IS 1080 shallow foundations".
